title.narrative: Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) for the IDPs in White Nile State

description.narrative: The ongoing crisis has increased the number of internally displaced people and refugees, in Kosti, Rabak, Aljabalain, Gutina, Guli and other localities in White Nile. To date, 656,068 displaced individuals are gathering in around 400 gathering locations around Kosti and the surrounding localities, with some living with relatives and those able to live in rented houses. The newly arrived IDPs have been allocated space in Goza Salaam, the main gathering point where they are camping. Most of the displaced people are children and women. Access challenges, road closures due to the on-and-off fighting and hyperinflation continue hitting civilian populations and further worsen the needs of the most vulnerable groups of people, including women, children and persons with disabilities. Persons with disabilities, and children, are too often left behind in situations of armed conflict and experience serious risks and challenges to flee to protect themselves and access necessities. Women and girls, as well as remaining at increased risk of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence (CRSV). Traditional practices, cultural beliefs and gender inequality further expose vulnerable people to protection risks, deeply affecting their mental and nutritional well-being. Several IDPs are traumatized, especially women and girls, reporting CRSV and have gone long without food, making them weak. Malnutrition among children less than five years and pregnant and breastfeeding women (PBW) among the displaced persons in the highlighted localities is high. Based on the SMART survey prioritization and revised Nutrition Response Prioritization (Nov-2024) which have been shared by Sudan national nutrition cluster, it is indicated that White Nile state, Kosti and Rabak have been categorised as priority 3 (IPC 3 and GAM <15%, IDP <30%) but El Gutain was categorized as priority 2 (IPC 4 and GAM <15%, IDP <30%) and the level of malnutrition is increasing as new secondary displacements and arrivals continue.
